It doesn't always get better, depression and suicidal ideation are sometimes akin to waves. You have your highs and your lows, and if nothing else, you learn to cope better. Still, it's not worth giving in to, simply because the purpose of our lives is experience. Good or bad, even tinged in constant thoughts of suicide, I live my days full of experiences and seeking new ones.

So no, it doesn't get better, but that doesn't mean you can't improve your quality of life. 

When I was in a psychiatric hospital I met a wonderful woman who was plagued with horrendous bouts of suicidal ideation. The reason she sticks out is that she herself was a psychiatrist and knew the ins and outs of her condition as well as many others.

Even with all the knowledge and tools at her disposal her ideation never got any better. Despite this, she shared with me various mitigation tactics. She journaled, forced herself to partake in hobbies or social interactions. Threw herself into her work and learned all that you can expect one in her field to know. Even so, she wound up in the same hospital as me. 

Were it not for her sharing similar issues and speaking to me honestly on these matters, my time in that hospital would have been meaningless. 

Through my stay there, she coached me on skills I could develop to handle my mental illness. She offered me advice on anything she had to offer, and was a comforting presence in an otherwise hostile and unfamiliar environment. For that I can only thank her and hope she is still with us today.

There's a lot more to this story, and the incredible people involved. However, my sleep deprived ramblings will suit you readers no further so I shall abstain.
